action_criteria.expected_evidence: Evans index 0.34, callosal angle 84 degrees, temporal horns enlarged, aqueduct patent, no obstruction, DESH absent; superficial siderosis; coil artefact, no new haemorrhage; Fazekas 1, MTA 1
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI with the NPH markers
action_criteria.rationale: After a coiled aneurysm and SAH, MRI must show communicating ventriculomegaly without obstruction, rebleeding or a new lesion before CSF is removed.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal blood count, sodium, creatinine, TSH and vitamin B12; RPR and HIV non-reactive
action_criteria.label: Targeted labs for reversible contributors
action_criteria.rationale: Blood tests do not diagnose NPH; they only screen for thyroid, B12, syphilis or metabolic contributors to the cognitive decline.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 28 s, 10-metre walk 22 s, magnetic shuffling gait with freezing, en-bloc turn, 2-step retropulsion
action_criteria.label: Baseline timed gait assessment before the tap
action_criteria.rationale: The tap response can only be judged against objective baseline TUG and 10-metre walk times recorded before CSF is removed.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MoCA 21/30 with executive, attention and fluency errors, free recall 2/5 improving to 4/5 with cues
action_criteria.label: Bedside cognitive screen
action_criteria.rationale: A baseline MoCA documents the executive and recall deficits and lets the post-tap score be compared with it.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Opening pressure 18 cmH2O, normal cells and glucose, protein 62 mg/dL; 40 mL removed; TUG 28 to 20 s at 24 hours (29%), 10-metre walk 22 to 16 s, MoCA 21 to 24
action_criteria.label: Lumbar tap test with opening pressure
action_criteria.rationale: A normal opening pressure and an objective gait response to CSF removal identify shunt-responsive communicating hydrocephalus after the SAH.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 22 s at 2 hours and 20 s at 24 hours (29%), 10-metre walk 16 s (27%), MoCA 24/30, no incontinence
action_criteria.label: Post-tap timed gait reassessment
action_criteria.rationale: Repeating the timed measures at 2 and 24 hours after the 40 mL tap shows whether his gait responds to CSF removal, the evidence for a shunt in hydrocephalus after the SAH.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not label the hydrocephalus idiopathic: the aneurysmal SAH with intraventricular extension is an antecedent that makes it secondary NPH [Relkin_2005]
Do not stop aspirin for the lumbar tap
Do not attribute the second decline to post-SAH depression or static SAH sequelae when the gait and continence improve after CSF removal
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve for secondary (post-aneurysmal SAH) communicating hydrocephalus, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 29% in TUG at 24 hours, the communicating ventriculomegaly with supportive MRI features and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Continue aspirin 81 mg through the lumbar tap; low-dose aspirin alone does not require interruption before lumbar puncture [ASRA_2025]
Continue sertraline and treat the post-SAH depression in parallel; depression does not explain the gait disorder or the response to CSF removal

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no role in a chronic gait and cognitive syndrome without seizures or fluctuating awareness
There is no syncope, palpitation or cardiac question in this gait and cognitive work-up
Echocardiography answers no question in this work-up: there is no cardioembolic event or heart failure
Head CT adds nothing once brain MRI is available, which measures the ventricles, callosal angle and DESH better
Rhythm monitoring has no role without syncope or a suspected arrhythmia
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are
Prion, inflammatory and infectious CSF assays answer no question in a chronic afebrile gait syndrome with normal CSF cells

accepted: Secondary normal pressure hydrocephalus, post-aneurysmal SAH (communicating hydrocephalus)

differential.key_features: The clinical and imaging picture matches, but the aneurysmal SAH with intraventricular extension is an antecedent, so the hydrocephalus is secondary.
Depressed affect is present, but depression does not produce a magnetic gait, ventriculomegaly or a 29% TUG improvement after CSF removal.
Siderosis follows the known SAH, but there is no hearing loss, cerebellar ataxia or pyramidal sign, and finger-nose testing is normal.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Deep white matter disease is only Fazekas grade 1 without lacunes.
No rest tremor, rigidity or bradykinesia; the lower-body gait disorder improved after CSF removal.
Hippocampi are preserved (MTA 1) and recall improves with cueing, an executive rather than amnestic profile.
Temporal horns enlarged out of proportion to the hippocampi, an acute callosal angle of 84 degrees and the response to CSF removal argue against atrophy.

key_clinical_evidence: Communicating hydrocephalus after an identified antecedent such as SAH is secondary NPH (ICD-10 G91.0), not iNPH, and is treated by the same shunt route [Relkin_2005]
Imaging: Evans index 0.34 without obstruction, with an acute callosal angle (84 degrees) and temporal horn enlargement; DESH is absent, as is common in secondary NPH [Nakajima_2021]
Normal opening pressure (18 cmH2O); TUG improved 29% at 24 hours after a 40 mL tap, above the 10% TUG improvement commonly used as a positive threshold (no guideline sets a single cut-off)
Tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% with PPV 73% to 100% [Marmarou_2005]
Low-dose aspirin alone does not need to be stopped before a lumbar puncture [ASRA_2025]

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Depression may slow cognition but does not cause a magnetic gait, urinary incontinence, ventriculomegaly or a gait response to CSF removal.
red_herrings.intended_effect: The second decline is attributed to post-SAH depression

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A good recovery followed by a new progressive decline 2 to 3 years later is not a static SAH sequela; delayed communicating hydrocephalus is the treatable cause.
red_herrings.data_point: Prior SAH (subarachnoid hemorrhage, aneurysmal, right posterior communicating artery aneurysm treated with coil embolization 4 years ago)
red_herrings.intended_effect: The decline is accepted as late sequelae of the SAH and not investigated

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]
The timed gait is repeated after the tap, at 2 to 24 hours, so that its change from the baseline measures the response to CSF removal [Nakajima_2021]

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 3 required (brain MRI, baseline timed gait, CSF tap test), 1 recommended (post-tap reassessment) and 2 optional (labs, cognitive screen) actions; 2 grounded red herrings; 7 differential alternatives.
metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Diagnostic puzzle: secondary NPH 4 years after aneurysmal SAH; post-SAH depression and the SAH itself as confounders; the label must be secondary, not idiopathic, and aspirin need not be stopped for the tap.

patient.history_present_illness: A 76-year-old retired professor with aneurysmal SAH (right posterior communicating artery aneurysm, treated by coil embolization 4 years ago) was referred by his neurosurgeon after a gradual but progressive deterioration in gait and cognition over the past 18 months. The hemorrhage was extensive, with thick basal subarachnoid blood and intraventricular extension (modified Fisher grade 4). His acute course was complicated by a 14-day ICU stay with cerebral vasospasm, treated with a 21-day course of oral nimodipine; his hypertension has since been treated with verapamil. He had a surprisingly good neurological recovery by 6 months and returned to limited academic consulting. However, over the past 18 months he has had a second decline: progressive shuffling gait, new urinary urgency with incontinence (2-3 episodes per week), and worsening memory and executive function. His son, a physician, has been tracking his father's decline and asked for a formal evaluation. A head MRI 3 months ago at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available.

neurological_exam.additional: No nuchal rigidity. No grasp reflex. Frontal lobe exam: minimal frontal release signs (snout positive).
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No papilledema. Pupils equal and reactive. The right third nerve palsy from the SAH has fully resolved.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, shuffling magnetic gait with short steps and freezing at the doorway. Cannot tandem walk. Pull test: 2 steps backward. Timed gait measures reported separately.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x3 (knows the date with prompting). Slowed processing, mildly depressed affect, no aphasia. Formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone. Full strength. No rigidity. No tremor.
